extracted.intended_audience: general public, students, policymakers, advocates, and researchers interested in U.S. net neutrality policy
extracted.subtask_description: Overview of policy options, legal tests, and arguments used to evaluate or design net neutrality regulation in the United States. Covers proposed bills, FCC classification options, state actions, and normative claims for and against regulation.

rubrics_metrics.name: Prohibition on FCC regulation (Internet Freedom Act)
rubrics_metrics.description: “The FCC shall not propose, promulgate, or issue any regulations regarding the Internet or IP-enabled services.”
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Language from S.1836 (Internet Freedom Act of 2009) — would prevent the FCC from imposing network/net neutrality rules on the Internet by statutory bar to FCC rulemaking.

rubrics_metrics.name: Congressional jurisdiction over Internet regulation (H.R.96)
rubrics_metrics.description: Regulation of the Internet is under the jurisdiction of Congress, not the FCC.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: H.R.96 (Internet Freedom Act) asserts congressional primacy to strike down FCC net neutrality rulemaking; frames proper evaluator as Congress rather than the agency.

rubrics_metrics.name: FCC may regulate only upon demonstrated market failure (H.R.166)
rubrics_metrics.description: Prohibit the FCC from regulating the Internet or information services unless there is demonstrated market failure.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: H.R.166 (Internet Investment, Innovation, and Competition Preservation Act) conditions regulatory authority on evidence of market failure, making market-failure demonstration a trigger for regulation.

rubrics_metrics.name: Codify FCC's six net neutrality principles (S.74)
rubrics_metrics.description: Codify the FCC's six net neutrality principles (outlined in a November 2009 FCC Notice of Proposed Rule Making).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: S.74 (Internet Freedom, Broadband Promotion, and Consumer Protection Act of 2011) would put the FCC's principles into statute as a basis for enforcement and policy clarity.

rubrics_metrics.name: Reclassification under Title II with forbearance ('Third Way')
rubrics_metrics.description: Narrowly reclassify Internet access as a telecommunication service under Title II of the Communications Act and apply only six common-carrier rules under the legal principle of forbearance.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Proposed by Commissioner Julius Genachowski as a way to give the FCC authority to prevent unreasonable discrimination while forbearance limits the scope of onerous regulation; supported by some (e.g., Google) and opposed by incumbents (e.g., AT&T).

rubrics_metrics.name: Hybrid regulatory approach (divide wholesale and retail transactions)
rubrics_metrics.description: Adopt a hybrid approach that divides 'wholesale' and 'retail' transactions — stricter regulation for data between content providers and ISPs and more lax rules between ISPs and consumers.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Suggested as a middle-ground solution that includes reclassification elements and Section 706; aims to tightly restrict fast lanes between content providers and ISPs while avoiding heavy-handed rules on ISP-to-consumer service.

rubrics_metrics.name: Prevent 'fast lanes' / prohibit preferential treatment for content providers
rubrics_metrics.description: Restrict or ban offering a data 'fast lane' that gives preferential treatment to certain content providers in exchange for fees.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Neutrality advocates argue fast lanes would let ISPs extract payment from content providers and create artificial scarcity and reduced competition; hybrid/Title II proposals often explicitly target fast lanes.

rubrics_metrics.name: Allow reasonable network management (avoid absurdities)
rubrics_metrics.description: Network neutrality rules must allow ISPs to engage in reasonable network-management practices (e.g., dropping spam, stopping attacks) without being criminalized by overly broad prohibitions.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Bram Cohen and others warn legislation should avoid absurd unintended consequences that would prevent ordinary operational traffic management; carve-outs for such management are necessary.

rubrics_metrics.name: Regulate only when significant market failure or consumer harm is demonstrated (FTC view)
rubrics_metrics.description: New regulations should be avoided absent a significant market failure or demonstrated consumer harm from broadband providers' conduct.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The FTC cautioned restraint, arguing premature regulation could reduce consumer welfare; this is used as a standard to decide whether intervention is warranted.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use existing Section 201(b) authority for targeted regulation
rubrics_metrics.description: Section 201(b) of the Communications Act could grant the Commission authority to regulate broadband where charges, practices, or regulations for common-carrier services are unjust and unreasonable.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Aparna Watal suggests using targeted existing statutory authority (Section 201(b)) as an alternative to broad reclassification, focusing enforcement where specific unjust/unreasonable practices occur.

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoid premature legislative mandates; prefer modest consumer-protection steps
rubrics_metrics.description: It is undesirable and premature to legislatively mandate network neutrality without strong evidence; instead consider modest consumer-protection rules.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Watal and others argue there have been few overt incidents and costs are limited, so measures like disclosure and easier switching may be preferable to paternalistic mandates.

rubrics_metrics.name: ISPs must disclose network management practices
rubrics_metrics.description: Require ISPs to disclose their network management practices to consumers.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Disclosure is proposed as a policing mechanism that lets consumers and the market punish or avoid anti-competitive management rather than immediate heavy regulation.

rubrics_metrics.name: Allow consumers to switch ISPs inexpensively
rubrics_metrics.description: Policies should make it inexpensive and easy for consumers to switch ISPs to increase market competition as a check on ISP behavior.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Lower switching costs strengthen market discipline and can serve as an alternative remedy to direct regulation.

rubrics_metrics.name: Beware cross-layer regulatory effects
rubrics_metrics.description: Regulating broadband pipelines can indirectly regulate the content and applications that run over them, producing a complex, overlapping, and fractured regulatory landscape.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Policymakers should consider how regulation of 'pipelines' affects higher Internet layers and avoid unintended broad impacts on content and applications.

rubrics_metrics.name: Clarify packet-priority exceptions for emergency/mission-critical services
rubrics_metrics.description: Decide whether voice packets or emergency/mission-critical (e.g., tele-medicine) applications should receive higher priority than other traffic.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This unresolved technical/policy question affects whether any prioritization carve-outs should be part of net neutrality rules; policymakers must balance QoS needs against neutrality principles.

rubrics_metrics.name: Municipal broadband as an alternative solution
rubrics_metrics.description: Promote municipal broadband networks as a possible solution to net neutrality concerns by offering alternative access providers.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Suggested by Susan Crawford and others as a competition-focused remedy to ISP abuses; subject to state-level legal and political constraints.

rubrics_metrics.name: Technological workarounds alone may be insufficient
rubrics_metrics.description: Technologies such as municipal wireless, encryption, onion routing, or time-shifting DVR may not be sufficient by themselves to render discrimination moot.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The article notes technical mitigations cannot fully substitute for policy/regulatory solutions in many contexts.

rubrics_metrics.name: States can enforce net neutrality via legislation and procurement
rubrics_metrics.description: Individual states may uphold net neutrality through statutes, executive orders, litigation, and by requiring state/local contracts to include net-neutral service terms.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Many states introduced bills and contractual requirements (e.g., SB-822 in California); state action is a parallel enforcement path with its own litigation risks.

rubrics_metrics.name: Prevent federal preemption that blocks municipal competition
rubrics_metrics.description: Be wary of federal preemption that would ban states or municipalities from competing in broadband markets; Supreme Court precedent allows some exceptions for states entering business for citizens.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Cable companies have lobbied for preemption; preserving municipal authority can be an explicit policy criterion to foster competition.

rubrics_metrics.name: Allow data discrimination to guarantee quality-of-service (opponent view)
rubrics_metrics.description: Permit some forms of data discrimination or prioritization to guarantee quality-of-service (QoS) for certain applications.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Opponents of strict neutrality argue QoS requirements (e.g., for real-time voice/video) justify limited discrimination and management practices.

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoid regulations that deter broadband investment (opponent concern re Title II)
rubrics_metrics.description: Regulatory approaches (notably Title II reclassification) should be avoided if they reduce incentives for broadband investment because providers may be unable to recover investments.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Incumbent and industry groups cite potential investment slowdowns as a reason to prefer lighter regulation or forbearance.

rubrics_metrics.name: Eminent domain or forced competition as an alternative
rubrics_metrics.description: Use eminent domain or other public measures to force competition among telecom providers rather than imposing new regulatory constraints.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Proposed by some commentators (e.g., Andy Kessler) as a market-structure remedy to poor service and lack of competition.

rubrics_metrics.name: Protect marginalized voices and civil-rights interests
rubrics_metrics.description: Net neutrality should be evaluated for its role in protecting communities of color and marginalized groups by preventing ISPs from blocking or discriminating against unpopular speech.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Civil rights groups argue neutrality preserves access to platforms for organizing and storytelling that mainstream media exclude; equity considerations are an explicit policy criterion.

rubrics_metrics.name: Prevent tiered service models that stifle startups and small businesses
rubrics_metrics.description: Avoid permitting tiered service models that allow established companies to pay for preferential access while stifling small businesses/startups that cannot afford such fees.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Proponents argue open access is necessary to preserve innovation and competition; economic impact on startups is an evaluative metric.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use enforcement and litigation to implement or restore rules
rubrics_metrics.description: Enforcement via rulemaking, state legislation (e.g., California SB-822), and litigation by states/attorneys-general are tools for implementing or restoring net neutrality protections.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The article documents state suits and federal orders (e.g., FCC Restoring Internet Freedom Order, state lawsuits) showing enforcement and courts are part of the policy mechanism.
